messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 24-year-old Latin American man who comes to therapy carrying himself with the careful composure of someone who has learned not to draw attention to pain. He works as a financial analyst now, a job that seems almost deliberately removed from the chaos of his earlier life: spreadsheets, quarterly reports, market trends, clean lines and predictable numbers. He says he likes how the work makes sense. Numbers do not surprise him. They do not scream. They do not suddenly change shape in the dark.

Before this life, he is deployed in combat, and that is where everything breaks open. He describes the days there as all edges and noise: dust in the mouth, sweat under heavy gear, the constant scan of rooftops and roadways, the sense that every ordinary movement could be the last. He is young enough then to still believe he will come home unchanged, and old enough to know better by the time the worst day arrives. He does not talk about that event in a linear way at first. He circles it. He starts with the weather, the heat, the smell of metal, the weight of his rifle. Then he stops, looks down, and says that one second is still happening to him.

What he remembers most is the helplessness. He recalls the sound before the explosion, the sudden violent shift from routine vigilance to pure terror, the bodies moving in ways they should not move, the blood he cannot wash out of his mind no matter how much time passes. In the aftermath, he does what many around him do: he keeps moving, keeps listening for orders, keeps his face blank. He learns quickly that there is no room for collapsing. He swallows the shock because everyone else is swallowing theirs. But from that point on, he begins living as if another blast could happen at any moment.

When he returns home, he expects relief and feels instead a strange emptiness. Civilian life is louder than he expects and somehow less safe. Fireworks on the Fourth of July make his heart race before he knows what is happening. A car backfiring in a parking garage drops him into a cold, immediate panic. He becomes someone who chooses his seat facing the door, who notices exits in restaurants, who scans rooftops during walks downtown. He says he does it automatically, without deciding to. His body is always ahead of his mind, already bracing. He sleeps poorly, and when he does fall asleep, he wakes drenched in sweat from dreams he cannot fully describe because they dissolve as soon as he opens his eyes. He avoids war movies, news coverage, and even conversations that drift toward military topics. He tells friends he is tired or busy. He is not sure how to explain that certain sounds make him feel as if the world is about to split open.

At work, he functions with impressive discipline. He is the kind of analyst coworkers trust because he is thorough and precise, but he pays a private price for that steadiness. He double-checks everything. He rereads emails repeatedly. He struggles to focus when a memory intrudes mid-task, and then he has to stare at the screen for several minutes before the numbers stop blurring. He has moments in meetings when he feels suddenly far away, as if the room has tilted and he is watching himself from a distance. He keeps his jaw tight, his shoulders raised, and by evening he is exhausted in a way that sleep does not fix. He has become irritable with people he cares about, though he often apologizes afterward and says he is under pressure. He does not date much. He says it is easier not to let people get close than to explain why he startles when someone touches his arm from behind.

Over time, the memories become less like memories and more like intrusions. They arrive uninvited: a smell, a flash of light, a sound in the street, and suddenly he is back there, feeling the same urgency, the same fear, the same certainty that death is near. He does not talk about this easily. He is embarrassed by how powerless it makes him feel. He prides himself on being disciplined, competent, in control. Yet in private he finds himself sitting in his car after work, unable to turn the key for several minutes because he needs to breathe and convince his body that he is not in danger. Sometimes he scrolls on his phone late into the night just to keep from thinking. Sometimes he drinks more than he means to, then regrets it the next morning when the anxiety returns sharper.

In session, he speaks with restraint, but there is grief beneath the restraint. He misses the version of himself who felt uncomplicated pride in enduring hard things. He is not only frightened; he is angry that the war followed him home and rearranged ordinary life into something narrow and vigilant. Even so, there are small moments when he sounds hopeful: when he talks about wanting to feel present again, when he describes the relief of naming what has been happening inside him, when he admits that part of him still expects to hear the blast and another part longs for a future in which he does not.
